# Zealot — Session Handover

This file tracks the task board for this repo. A prior `handover.md`
existed in this repo's history but was removed (commit `4996098`, "Remove
handover.md") and is not carried forward here — task statuses below for
Tasks 6, 7 and 9 are as reported by the operator, not re-derived from that
removed file or independently re-verified against the code.

**Debugging the Task 40 pipeline, Render or the storage repo? Read `docs/ci/operator-runbook.md` first.** It records every command, route, value and gotcha found in the 2026-10-05 operator session, so nothing has to be rediscovered.

**Before rediscovering what exists, read the entry "Pipeline audit" at the top of the Session log (2026-10-06).** It lists what is installed, what is set, what is missing and what comes next, so a session can start from the next step.

## Handoff process — ONE combined patch, apply with `git am` + `git push`

**Standing rule for every session (operator's instruction, supersedes any
older apply block further down this file):**

1. Session does the work on a branch, never pushes directly to `develop`/`main`.
2. **Deliver exactly ONE `.patch` file — a single combined commit.** Everything
   the session changed goes into it: app code, specs, locale files **and** the
   `handover.md` update (task board, status marks, session log). Squash the
   session's work into one commit on top of `develop`, then run
   `git format-patch -1 HEAD`. Never hand over a numbered series
   (`0001…000n`), never a separate "docs" patch, never several files the
   operator has to order. If the session did several TSF slices, they all ride
   in this one commit; list the slices in the commit body.
3. **The operator's checkout is already in place and up to date, so applying is
   just this — no `checkout`, no `pull`, no `status` dance:**
   ```
   cd ~/zealot
   git am ~/storage/downloads/<the-one-patch>.patch
   git push
   ```
   The session names the exact file it is handing over. Before handing it
   over the session must confirm the patch applies cleanly (`git apply --check`
   / a throwaway `git am`) against the `develop` tip it cloned. `git am` fails
   loudly if the tree has diverged since the patch was generated; if that
   happens, don't force it — the operator reports back and the next session
   rebases the patch instead of resolving conflicts blind. If a *previous*
   patch from this file's history was only partly applied, say so before
   generating a new one — a combined patch built on the wrong base will not
   apply.
   (Older task-board entries below still show the previous
   `git checkout develop && git pull` block and multi-patch sequences; those
   are historical — follow this section, not them.)
4. **After the push, check the RIGHT workflow** — `Anthropic - Build & Deploy
   develop` (two jobs: Build & push image to GHCR → Trigger Render deploy),
   not whatever run is listed on top. See "Which workflow is the deploy
   pipeline?" below before reporting any build/deploy status.
5. Build/behavior is verified after that push (CI, or a manual smoke test),
   not claimed as verified by the session itself — nothing in this session
   was run through Ruby/Node locally (no Ruby/Node runtime in the sandbox
   this was written in), so treat everything below as **code-complete,
   not syntax- or build-checked**.

## Task-splitting formula (TSF) — how every task on this board gets cut into patches

Added with Task 14. Use it for any task bigger than one obvious change, and
write the resulting slice table into the task's board entry *before* any code
is written. The goal is that each patch is small enough for the operator to
apply from Termux, verify in two minutes, and revert alone if it misbehaves.

**Slice test — a slice is only valid if it passes all five:**

1. **One behaviour.** The goal fits in one sentence with no "and". If it
   needs an "and", it is two slices.
2. **Small.** Roughly ≤ 6 files and ≤ 300 changed lines, ideally one layer
   (view · controller/model · JS+CSS · locale). Over that → split again.
3. **Bootable after every slice.** Never leave a view calling a helper a
   previous slice deleted. Removals land *after* their replacement exists.
4. **Checkable.** Has a ≤ 2-minute browser check for the operator **and** a
   machine check where the sandbox allows (`ruby -c`, a spec, `pnpm exec vite
   build`). Anything not checkable in the sandbox is written down as
   "not verified", per this file's standing convention.
5. **Reversible.** Each slice lists what to revert (files / hunks) so it can be
   backed out on its own even though a session ships as one combined commit; no
   slice depends on a data migration unless it says so.

**Ordering formula** (apply top to bottom, ties broken by lowest risk first):

1. ❓ decisions resolved by the operator → nothing is built on a guess.
2. Foundation before UI (routes/controllers/models before the views using them).
3. Replacement before removal (new login path before deleting the old one).
4. Independent low-risk slices before cross-cutting ones (footer before nav).
5. Purely additive data slices (lists, copy) last — they never block anything.
6. The docs/status update (🆕 → ✅) is always the last edit of a session and
   goes into the same single patch.

**Slice card** (one per slice, in the task entry): `ID · Goal · Depends on ·
Files (predicted) · Acceptance check · Verify · Risk`.

**Naming & delivery:** Task `N` → slices `Na, Nb, …`. Slices are *planning and
verification units*, not separate patches. Branch `feat/task-N-<slug>` off
`develop`; the session's slices are squashed into **one** commit
(`feat(task-N): <slices done>`), delivered as **one** patch per the Handoff
process at the top of this file. A session should take **1–3 slices**, never
more than it can honestly verify. Every slice that changes copy updates
`en.yml` and `zh-CN.yml` together (or says it didn't).

## ⚠️ Which workflow is the deploy pipeline? (read before touching CI or telling the operator "the build passed")

**There is exactly ONE deploy pipeline: `Anthropic - Build & Deploy develop`
(`.github/workflows/anthropic_deploy_main.yml`).** It has **two jobs, in
this order**, and this is what a correct run looks like in the Actions UI:

```
Build & push image to GHCR  ──►  Trigger Render deploy
        (~3–4 min)                      (~5 s)
```

Anything else in the Actions tab is **not** the deploy, no matter how
recent or how prominent it looks. In particular, a run whose graph is a
*single* box titled **"Push Docker image to multiple registries"** is
`Publish Nightly Docker Image` — an upstream leftover, **not** the pipeline
that ships to Render.

### What went wrong (and why it kept happening)

Every push to `develop` used to start **two** workflows in the same
second: the real pipeline above, and `publish_nighty.yml`. GitHub's
Actions list sorted the Nightly run **above** the real one (e.g. run
`Publish Nightly #20` sat on top of `Anthropic - Build & Deploy #38` for
commit `4bc3c7a`), so the operator opened the top run, saw a one-job graph
that did not match the known-good one, and concluded "the wrong workflow is
running" — repeatedly (this is the same confusion recorded in the
"Confirmed & closed" entry below, which blamed it on `publish_nighty.yml`).
The real pipeline was in fact running and green each time.

Nightly was also actively harmful beyond confusing people: its
multi-arch (amd64 + arm64 via QEMU) build ran ~5 min in parallel and
competed with the real build for runner capacity (`test_docker_build.yml`'s
header comment records an earlier session observing exactly this kind of
starvation).

### Fix (this session)

`publish_nighty.yml` is now **`workflow_dispatch` (manual) only** — it no
longer runs on push. After this patch, **a normal push to `develop` starts
only `Anthropic - Build & Deploy develop`.** Verified before changing it that
nothing depends on the `nightly` tag: `render.yaml` pulls
`ghcr.io/zapier-codes/zealot:deploy-latest` / `deploy-<sha>` (published only
by `anthropic_deploy_main.yml`), and `fly.toml`'s `:nightly` image is
**upstream's** `tryzealot/zealot`, not this fork's.

### What triggers on `develop` now

| Workflow (file) | Fires on push to `develop`? | Shape | Is it the deploy? |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Anthropic - Build & Deploy develop** (`anthropic_deploy_main.yml`) | **Yes, every push** (except docs-only: `**.md`, `.devcontainer/`, `.vscode/`, `LICENSE`) | 2 jobs: Build & push → Trigger Render deploy | **YES — the only one** |
| Publish Nightly Docker Image (`publish_nighty.yml`) | **No** — manual only since this fix | 1 job: "Push Docker image to multiple registries" | No |
| Publish Codespace Docker Image (`publish_codespace.yml`) | Only if `package.json`, `pnpm-lock.yaml`, `Gemfile*`, `yarn.lock`, `.mise.toml`, `.devcontainer/Dockerfile.base` or that workflow file changed (can run 10–25 min) | 1 job: "Push Codespace Docker image to multiple registries" | No |
| CI - RSpec, tests only (`ci_rspec.yml`) | **No** — pull requests and manual (`workflow_dispatch`) only | 2 jobs: "RSpec (PostgreSQL 16)" and "db/schema.rb matches migrations" | No (builds no image, never touches Render) |
| Sync README to Organization (`sync_readme.yml`) | Only if `README.md` changed | 1 job | No |
| Publish Preview (`publish_preview.yml`) | No — `release/*` branches only | 1 job | No |
| Publish Release (`publish_release.yml`) | No — version tags only | 1 job | No |
| Test Docker Build (`test_docker_build.yml`) | No — pull requests only | 1 job | No (dry-run check) |

If a push touches dependency files you will still see **Publish Codespace**
appear next to the real pipeline. That is expected, is not the deploy, and
can be ignored. (It was left alone deliberately; if the operator wants it
manual-only as well, it is the same one-line trigger change.)

### Rules for every future session

1. **Never tell the operator "the deploy passed/failed" from a run you have
   not confirmed is `Anthropic - Build & Deploy develop`.** Check the
   workflow name at the top of the run page and that both jobs
   (`Build & push image to GHCR`, `Trigger Render deploy`) exist.
2. **Never re-add `push:` (or `branches: [develop]`) to
   `publish_nighty.yml`, `publish_preview.yml` or `test_docker_build.yml`**
   to "get a build". They are not the deploy path and re-adding them
   recreates this exact confusion (and burns runner minutes).
3. **Do not add a new workflow that triggers on push to `develop`** without
   updating the table above and giving it a name that cannot be mistaken for
   the deploy pipeline. Two workflows racing on the same push is how this
   started.
4. **How the operator (and you) should find the right run fast:** open
   `https://github.com/Zapier-codes/zealot/actions/workflows/anthropic_deploy_main.yml`
   — that URL lists *only* the deploy pipeline's runs. Or, in the Actions
   tab's left sidebar, tap **"Anthropic - Build & Deploy develop"** to filter.
   Don't judge by the top row of "All workflows".
5. **A green run still only proves GitHub got a 2xx back from Render's
   deploy hook.** Render's own Events/Deploys tab is the source of truth for
   whether the new image is actually live (see the closed pipeline entry
   below).
6. **Only the two `deploy-*` tags matter to Render.** Don't retarget
   `render.yaml` at `nightly`/`preview`/`latest`.
7. **How a session can check this itself:** the Actions pages are readable
   without auth via `web_fetch` (start from
   `https://github.com/Zapier-codes/zealot/actions`; the unauthenticated
   REST API is rate-limited from the sandbox). Each run page states the
   workflow file, status, and job list.

## Debug fixes (operator-directed, no task number)

### 2026-10-03 — production boot crash: `Unknown validator: 'MessageValidator'` (Render deploy `dep-db08doad0e5s73ahd1ag`, image `deploy-0669b07`)

**Read from the operator's uploaded log** (`render-deploy-dep-db08doad0e5s73ahd1ag.log`, saved with D-Store's `scripts/fetch-ci-log.sh`), not guessed. The migrations are fine: `30-zealot-upgrade` printed "Zealot database is up to date: 20261001100000" and every init script exited 0. What fails is Puma loading the app: `ArgumentError: Unknown validator: 'MessageValidator'` at `app/models/listing_edit.rb:37`, repeated about every 65 seconds (the supervisor restarts Zealot each time) until Render gives up after about 15 minutes and marks the deploy `update_failed`. Production eager-loads every model at boot, so a model that cannot load stops the whole app.

**Cause:** `validates :app_id, uniqueness: {...}, if: ..., message: '...'` has `message:` at the top level of `validates`, where Rails reads every unknown key as a validator name. Written in task 30a (2026-09-27, commit `010fc333`) and never loaded by Rails until a production boot, because 30a's code was "written, not run". **Fix:** `message:` moved inside the `uniqueness` hash; `spec/models/listing_edit_spec.rb` now checks the message. A scan of every `validates` call under `app/` found no other top-level `message:`, `minimum`, `in`, `with` or `scope` keys; that scan was a text pattern, not Rails, so it does not prove the app loads. **Not run** (no Ruby here, no-testing instruction): the first proof is the next Render deploy reaching `live`; if the log shows another boot error, upload it the same way.

**Also in that log, not causes:** `fix-attrs.d 11-crontab-dir: exited 1` (harmless as the boot continues), `SMTP is not configure, skip`, and the `No open ports detected` lines, which only mean Puma had not bound yet. `warning: already initialized constant ListingEdit::LISTING_FIELDS` appears once per attempt, a side effect of the failed load being retried. Every earlier `update_failed` deploy back to 2026-09-29 may share this cause; their logs were not read.

## Task board

### 🧭 Play-parity program — Tasks 28–37 (Task 37 added this session; docs only; nothing below is built)

*Read Task 28 first. Tasks 29–36 are listed in phase order, not newest-first. Every slice follows the TSF; every ❓ is for the operator, not for a session to guess.*

#### 🆕 Task 28: Play-parity architecture — plane map, principles and phases (umbrella, no code)

**Operator direction.** Mirror the Play Console / Play Store concept, revamp the architecture fully around it, and rival the industry giants. The store is populated through the Aptoide MCP, and **the home page always shows Zealot's apps first** (recorded under Task 9).

**Provenance.** The plane model below is the session's analysis of how Google Play is organized, drawing on Task 27's earlier research (Google Play Console/Developer API, Apple, Huawei, Samsung, F-Droid). It was **not re-read source by source this session**. Verify against Google's own docs before relying on a specific behavior, most of all Android's rules for unattended updates, which Task 32 depends on.

**Play as separate planes** (the console and the store never share a runtime; they exchange only signed, versioned artifacts):

| Plane | Play | Here | State today |
|---|---|---|---|
| Control | Play Console + Publishing API: developer identity, app record, listing, content declarations, releases, reviews | Zealot | Partly built (Tasks 24, 25, 27a); index signing/publishing (27b) and the rest planned |
| Build and signing | Play App Signing + bundles, per-device splits | Zealot (org key vs upload key) | Built |
| Trust | Automated policy checks, then a human review queue | Zealot | Not built (Task 30) |
| Serving | Read-only store backend, search, compatibility filtering, CDN | D-store | UI on dummy data; reads the index once 5.g lands |
| Client | The Play Store app: installer sessions, background updates, on-device verification | D-Store Updater | Not built (Task 32) |
| Feedback | Ratings, reviews, Android vitals back to the console | D-store to Zealot | Not built (Tasks 31b, 33) |

**Principles to copy:**
1. The console never serves users; the store never accepts developer input. (Have it.)
2. Upload key is not the distribution key. (Have it: `PlayUploadKey` vs `AndroidSigningKey`.)
3. Publishing is a transactional edit: change a copy, validate, commit or discard. (Task 30a.)
4. Tracks: internal, closed, open, production. The store shows production only. (Task 30b.)
5. Everything a client trusts is signed and verifiable. (27b, Task 35a.)
6. The store only shows what will install on the device, so the catalog carries compatibility metadata. (Task 29.)
7. Automated checks before humans: permission diffs, signing-certificate continuity, scans. (Task 30c/30d.)
8. A feedback loop back to developers. (Tasks 31b, 33.)
9. The client is the trust anchor. This is the largest gap in the current plan: a web page can only download an APK, while an installed Updater can verify the index signature, the APK SHA-256 and the signing fingerprint on the device and can update in the background where Android permits it. (Task 32.)

**Phases (recommended order):**
- **Phase 1, trust core:** 27b-i/ii/iii, Task 29, D-store `5.g.i.zi`/`5.g.i.zo`/`5.g.iv`.
- **Phase 2, console parity:** 27c–27f, Task 30, Task 31.
- **Phase 3, client and feedback:** Task 32, Task 33, Task 34.
- **Phase 4, scale and trust:** Task 35, Task 36.
- **Phase 5, multi-tenant:** Task 37 *(cross-repo operator decision; 37b-i — host→tenant resolution, Rack layer — built, see below; 37b-ii-t1 — the `Tenant` table and model — built, see below; 37b-ii-t2 — the DB-backed, cached registry — built, see below; 37b-ii-k2 — the `TenantSigningKey` table and model, and 37b-ii-k3 — its lifecycle service — built, see below (no callers yet); 37b-ii-t3 — the non-key tenant admin views — built, see below; 37b-ii-k4 — `CatalogIndex::KeyResolver` — and 37b-ii-k5 — signing with every key valid in a rotation overlap — built, see below (the default tenant's output is unchanged; `Publish` refuses a non-default tenant until 37b-iii); 37b-ii-k6 — admin actions for the tenant key lifecycle — and 37b-ii-k7 — the key panel on the tenant edit page — built, see below (code-complete, request spec never run); 37b-iii — scoping the index and publish pipeline by tenant — is cut into s1–s7 below, **s1–s5, s6a and s7a built, s7 survey done (code-complete, never run under Rails or Postgres; s2's migration is on `develop`, s6a's is new), ❓1 and ❓3 resolved, s6b next (needs the operator's call on the new ❓3a)**; 37a's doc mirror and 37c are still open; **Task 38 (recursive "tree house" tenant hierarchy) — ❓5–❓9 resolved, slices written, none built yet; design revised to a recursive query with no closure table, Supabase considered and declined**)*.

**Catalog sources (operator rule):** first-party = Zealot's signed index; third-party = Aptoide via MCP. First-party is always first on the home page. Third-party apps are labelled as such, download from Aptoide (not Zealot), and never carry Zealot's verified/fingerprint claims. If the same package is in both, the Zealot entry wins. D-store owns the merge (`5.h`).

**Honest limits:** workflows and the trust model can match Play. Its ML malware detection, device attestation and scale cannot be matched, and its OS-level trust depends on Google's platform. The differentiator is transparency: an open, verifiable index and on-device APK verification.

**❓ Decisions (operator):**
1. Updater before or after the Phase 2 console features? (Recommendation: Phase 2 first; the Updater's verification code depends on the index being stable.)
2. Confirm the recommended answers recorded under Task 27 (❓1, ❓4, ❓6 refinement) and in the D-store handover.
3. Which Aptoide MCP: the official `Aptoide/aptoide-mcp` (Python, MIT, listed on Aptoide's GitHub, last updated Feb 12, 2026) or the third-party "Aptoide Ultimate API" actor on Apify (pay-per-query, hosted by Apify). Neither was inspected beyond its public listing this session.
4. Aptoide's terms for re-presenting its catalog and linking to its downloads: not checked. Confirm before building `5.h.ii` in D-store.

#### 🟡 Task 29: Catalog index v2 — the fields D-store and the Updater actually need (Phase 1) (29a, 29b, 29c, 29d, 29e done)

D-store's `App` type needs fields index v1 doesn't carry (found by comparing `lib/mock-data.ts` with `docs/catalog_index_v1.md`). Nothing consumes v1 yet (27a is not published anywhere), so revising now costs nothing; after 27b signs and publishes, every change is a migration.

**Fields to add (proposal; D-store signs off through its `5.g.i.zo`):**
- Per app: immutable `slug` (rule: never changes once live), `summary`, `category` (fixed vocabulary shared by both repos — originally proposed as D-store's then-current 12-item list; superseded by 29e's full Play-parity list, see that entry), `license`, `links` (site, source, tracker, donate), `available_regions`, `created_at`/`updated_at`.
- Listing declarations: `content_rating`, `data_safety` (collects data, data types, shared with third parties, encrypted in transit, deletion requests), `contains_ads`, `has_in_app_purchases`.
- Developer block: name, bio, profile URL, joined date.
- Compatibility: min and target SDK, ABIs, screen densities, required features, permissions. Zealot's `releases` table has no dedicated columns for these today, so extraction from the APK is new work (29c).
- `versions[]` instead of only `latest_version`: version name and code, download URL, SHA-256, size, signing fingerprint, changelog, release date, and a per-version `status` (`available`, `halted`, `pulled`). D-store's version history and rollback leaves (`5.c.ii`, `5.c.iii`) need this.
- Editorial, top level: `editorial` per app (`featured`, `editors_pick`), `sponsored_slots[]`, `collections[]` (authored in Task 31a).
- Index-level: `schema_version`, `generated_at`, a strictly increasing `sequence`, and `expires_at` (freshness, so a stale index can be refused).
- Not in the index, by design: install and view counts, average rating and rating count (store-owned).

publish path. Spec rewritten alongside (`spec/services/catalog_index/serializer_spec.rb`)
using the same real-`App`/real-`Release` approach as the v1 spec (no
factory for `Release`, built by hand against `db/schema.rb`'s non-null
columns) — adds cases for the envelope fields, multiple releases per app,
and the two slug cases below.

**Two things flagged rather than silently built past, per this file's own
"❓ decisions resolved by the operator" rule:**
1. **`sequence` is not really wired up.** The v2 doc says "27b/29b wires
   this up"; 29b's own predicted-files list only names the serializer, so
   this slice added `sequence:`/`expires_at:` as plain keyword args (default
   `sequence: 0`, `expires_at:` a new `DEFAULT_TTL` of 24h past
   `generated_at` if the caller doesn't supply one) rather than reaching
   into `Signer`/`CatalogIndexSigningKey` to persist a real counter.
   **`Signer.call` still doesn't pass a sequence, so every published index
   today would carry `sequence: 0`** — schema-valid but not yet doing the
   rollback-detection job the field exists for. The natural next slice
   (call it 29b-ii, or fold into 27b's remaining work) is: add a
   `last_sequence` column next to `CatalogIndexSigningKey#last_signed_at`,
   advance it under the same row lock, and have `Signer` pass it through.
   Not done here — flagging instead of guessing at the DB migration this
   session wasn't asked to make.
2. **`slug` is derived, not persisted.** It's the one v2 field the schema
   does not allow `null` for, so leaving it unset wasn't an option the way
   it was for `summary`/`category`/etc. `Serializer#slug_for` computes a
   deterministic, schema-valid slug from the app's *current* `name`
   (parameterized; falls back to `app-<id>` for a name with no alphanumeric
   characters — see the "falls back to app-<id>" spec case) every time the
   index is generated. This is **not** the real slug the v2 doc's "The slug
   rule" describes: it is not frozen at first go-live, so renaming an app
   changes its slug, which is exactly what that rule says must never
   happen once live. Whoever picks up Task 30's listing-edit machinery
   needs to add a persisted `slug` column, generate it once
   (collision-checked) the first time `listing_status` reaches `live`, and
   have the serializer prefer the persisted value — at which point
   `slug_for`'s derivation becomes the fallback for apps that predate that
   migration, not the only path.

#### 🟡 Task 30: Console publishing parity — edits, tracks, policy checks, review (Phase 2) (30a, 30b, 30f done)

Play's publishing model is a transactional edit on top of tracks, with automated checks and then a review queue. Zealot today has `go_live!` (Task 25) and channels.

| ID | Goal | Depends on | Files (predicted) | Acceptance check | Risk |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 30a ✅ | Staged listing edits: change a copy of the listing, validate, then commit or discard (the layer under the 27e editor) | 29a | model, service, policy, spec | Uncommitted edits never appear in the index; commit is one transaction; discard leaves the live listing untouched | medium |
| 30b ✅ | Map channels to tracks (internal, closed, open, production); only production feeds the index | 30a | `Channel`/`App`, index scope, spec | A release on a non-production track is absent from the index | medium |
| 30c 🟡 (cut into 30c-a…d below; **30c-a ✅**) | Automated checks on commit: permission diff against the previous version, signing-certificate continuity per package, package-name squatting check, malware-scan hook | 29c, 30a | service, spec | A version signed with a different key than earlier versions of the same package is blocked with a reason | medium |
| 30d | Manual review queue in admin: in review, approved, rejected with reason; only approved versions reach the index | 30c | model, views, locales, policy | A rejected version never appears in the index; the owner sees the reason | medium |
| 30e | Hold-until-release, halt and rollback | 27c | this is slice 27f; not duplicated here | see 27f | medium |
| 30f ✅ | Staged rollout: gate a release to a device-bucketed percentage of installs, ramp/halt/complete without re-uploading — Play-Console parity | 27c | model, migration, serializer, docs | Raising the percentage only ever adds devices in, never removes one already included; the same device always lands in the same bucket for a given release | medium |

**30b status (this session): `Channel`/`App`/index-scope shipped; no admin UI to pick a channel's track (same split 30a and 30f session 1 both used — data model and the scope that actually matters for the index first, an admin control as a follow-up if the operator wants channel creation/edit forms updated before 27e's editor exists anyway).**
- **Resolves this task's own recorded ❓** ("how Zealot's existing channels map to tracks — confirm against the `Channel` model before 30b"): there was nothing to map from — `Channel` had no publishing-related concept at all before this session (`device_type`, `download_filename_type`, `bundle_id`, none of them about pre-release vs. public distribution). This session adds `track` as a new enum column rather than inferring it from anything existing.
- `AddTrackToChannels` migration: `channels.track` (string enum, default `'production'`, plus a Postgres check constraint restricting it to the four Play-parity values). Defaulting to `production` (not `internal`, which is what a brand-new channel "should" probably start as under a real Play-parity workflow) is deliberate: every channel that exists today was, in practice, already being treated as production by `App#catalog_releases` before this session (there was no track concept to exclude anything with), so defaulting to anything quieter would silently drop every existing app's releases out of the next published index the moment this migration runs. Same "nothing disappears just because this slice shipped" reasoning 30f's `rollout_percentage`/`rollout_status` defaults already used.
- `Channel`: `enum :track, { internal:, closed:, open:, production: }, prefix: :track`, ordered loosest-audience-first to match Play Console's own track list, plus a `validates :track, presence:, inclusion:` matching the existing `device_type` validation's shape immediately above it.
- `App#catalog_releases` (the only caller of `catalog_releases` anywhere in the app -- checked; it exists solely to feed `CatalogIndex::Serializer`) now filters to `production`-track channels via a new `#production_channel_ids`. Every *other* caller of `#channel_ids` (`recently_release`, the dashboard, teardown, the Play-publish-exists check) is deliberately untouched and stays track-unscoped -- those are all management-facing views of an app's own uploads, which rightly still show internal/closed/open builds; only the public, signed index should ever be track-filtered. Covered by a spec asserting `#recently_release` still sees an internal-track release that `#catalog_releases` correctly excludes.
- `spec/models/app_catalog_releases_track_spec.rb` (new): the default-to-production case, production-only inclusion, exclusion of each non-production track, a mixed-track app returning only its production release, the "other callers stay unscoped" case above, and that assigning an out-of-enum track raises. Built directly against `App`/`Scheme`/`Channel` (no factories for the latter two exist in this repo -- checked `spec/factories/`), same pattern `spec/policies/app_ownership_spec.rb` already uses; `Release` built and persisted with `save!(validate: false)` to skip the unrelated create-only `file` presence validation, same workaround `29c`'s specs already established for the same reason.

**Explicitly NOT done this session:** no admin UI for setting a channel's track on create/edit (`ChannelsController`/its form) -- every channel created through the existing UI today still gets `production` by the column default, which is correct current behavior, not a broken state; a form control is only needed once someone wants to deliberately create an internal/closed/open channel, which nothing in the running app does yet. No migration of *existing* rows beyond the column default (there is no data to migrate in a fresh `db:schema:load`, and this sandbox never runs migrations against a real database regardless). No change to `30c`/`30d` (checks/review queue) even though they will eventually care which track a release lands on -- out of scope for this slice, matching the task table's own dependency ordering.

Errors are filtered to only the keys this edit staged, so an unrelated pre-existing problem on the live app's own data doesn't block a draft that never touched that field (covered by a spec forcing a stale invalid `play_package_name` via `update_column`). A second validation rejects any staged key outside `LISTING_FIELDS`.
- One draft per app, enforced twice: a model-level `uniqueness` validation scoped to `status: 'draft'` (committed/discarded rows don't count), and a matching Postgres partial unique index (`where: "status = 'draft'"`) so two concurrent requests can't race into two drafts that later disagree.
- `#commit!`: one transaction (`app.update!(staged_attributes)` then marking the edit `committed`), returns `false` rather than raising on an invalid edit or a non-draft edit — same "check the return value" shape `Release`'s own `enum`-backed saves use elsewhere in this codebase. `#discard!` never touches `app` at all, so "discard leaves the live listing untouched" is true by construction rather than something that has to be separately checked. Committing an edit with nothing staged is a harmless no-op success (marks it committed, changes nothing) rather than an error, since an editor opening then closing 27e's future UI without changing anything shouldn't be treated as a failure.
- Deliberately does **not** duplicate `App#publish_catalog_index_if_needed`: `commit!` calls the plain `app.update!`, which already fires that `after_commit` hook on its own, so a committed listing edit republishes the index exactly the way any other listing edit already does today — no new index-publishing code needed for this slice.
- `ListingEditService` (new, `app/services/listing_edit_service.rb`): the app-facing entry point 27e's future controller calls instead of `@app.update` directly — `#draft` (find-or-create the app's one draft), `#stage(attributes)` (merge into it, silently dropping any non-listing key rather than raising, so a controller can hand it a raw permitted-params hash that also carries other fields), `#commit!`/`#discard!` (thin delegation to the `ListingEdit` methods above). Kept separate from the model deliberately: the model owns the state machine and the "correct regardless of caller" transactional guarantees; the service is the ergonomic, params-shaped entry point on top of it.
- `ListingEditPolicy` (new): same `any_manage?` (`manage?(app:)`) rule `AppPolicy#update?` and `ReleasePolicy` already use — staging/committing/discarding is exactly as sensitive as editing the app directly, since it *is* how the app gets edited once 27e exists, so it gets no looser a check than `@app.update` has today.
- `App`: `has_many :listing_edits, dependent: :destroy` plus a `#draft_listing_edit` convenience reader. No other `App` change — `publish_catalog_index_if_needed` needed no touch, per the point above.
- `spec/models/listing_edit_spec.rb`, `spec/services/listing_edit_service_spec.rb`, `spec/factories/listing_edit.rb` (new): key-allowlisting, the dry-run-validation error-filtering behavior (including the stale-data case above), one-draft-per-app (and that committed/discarded rows don't count against it), `#commit!`/`#discard!` including the invalid-edit, non-draft, and empty-draft paths, and `ListingEditService`'s merge-not-replace staging and editor-recording. Built with real `create`/`build` against the `app`/`user` factories (both already exist, unlike `Release`, so no `.new` + `db/schema.rb` workaround was needed here the way `release_parser_spec.rb` used).

**Explicitly NOT done this session:** no controller or views — there is no 27e editor yet for this layer to sit under, so nothing calls `ListingEditService` in the running app today; this slice is purely the foundation 27e's controller will call into. No admin/owner-facing way to see a pending draft outside the Rails console or a future 27e view. No handling for what happens to an app's open draft if the app itself is destroyed beyond the plain `dependent: :destroy` on the association (no explicit spec for that cascade). Rate limiting or "who else is editing this listing right now" concurrency UX (two people staging conflicting drafts) is left to 27e, not this layer — the one-draft-per-app rule stops two *drafts* from existing, not two people editing the same one.

**31b result (slices 31b-a and 31b-b, one session, written, never run).** *31b-a:* `DstoreStats` (`app/services/dstore_stats.rb`, new): `DstoreStats.fetch` makes one `GET` to `DSTORE_STATS_URL` with `Authorization: Bearer <DSTORE_STATS_TOKEN>` (plain Faraday, 5 s open and 10 s read timeouts, no redirect following, no retry, a 1 MiB body cap) and returns a `Result` (`status` one of `:ok`, `:not_configured`, `:unauthorized` for 401/403, `:unavailable` for any other status or a network error, `:invalid` for non-JSON, a wrong shape or an oversized body; it never raises). Unset or blank config, or a URL that is not `https` (`http` only for `localhost`/`127.0.0.1`), is `:not_configured`, with no request made. `DstoreStats::Document.parse` checks the document against D-store's `store_stats()` contract (`generated_at`; `traffic`, `searches`, `reports`, `reviews`; counts are non-negative integers, `average_rating` is null or 0 to 5) and returns a new Hash holding **only the contract keys**, so a stray `comment`, `details` or `ip_hash` could not reach a view. The token is never in the result, a view or an error message. `spec/services/dstore_stats_spec.rb` (new). *31b-b:* `Admin::DstoreStatsController#index` (read-only; the admin namespace gates it, same as `Admin::DatabaseAnalyticsController`), route `admin/dstore_stats` (`index` only), a sidebar link under the admin section, `app/views/admin/dstore_stats/index.html.slim` (traffic, searches, ratings and report counts as cards and tables; each non-ok status shows one plain sentence and no figures), and `admin.dstore_stats` in `en.yml` and `zh-CN.yml`. **No migration, no write action, no model.**

**31b - choices flagged, not silently made:** (1) the endpoint is one full URL (`DSTORE_STATS_URL`), not a base URL plus a path, so a change to D-store's route is one env change; (2) a response that does not match the contract shows nothing (`:invalid`) rather than a partial page; (3) the page fetches live on every load, with no cache and no job, which is fine for one admin and would need a cache before it is shown to many; (4) `:unauthorized` tells the admin the token does not match, which is a hint about config, not a secret; (5) no `authorize` call, matching `Admin::DatabaseAnalyticsController`; the routing constraint (`user.admin?`) is the only gate; (6) the page is not tenant-scoped, because D-store's figures are per storefront, not per tenant. (7) **The endpoint is `/api/stats` on D-store, not `/api/admin/stats`.** D-store's first version of the route sat under `/api/admin/`, which its middleware puts behind a shared-password Basic gate that would have refused this client's bearer token; D-store's `5.g.v.zo` session moved it, so the example `DSTORE_STATS_URL` is `https://<d-store host>/api/stats`.

There is no Ruby or Rails in the authoring sandbox (`ruby` not found), so nothing was run, `ruby -c` included: the service, the controller, the spec and the Slim view are written, not checked. **Decisions (all four ✅ answered by the session on the operator's instruction: "answer them using industry standards"; the operator has not separately confirmed them, so each is overrulable, but the next session builds on them as written and does not ask).**

**Provenance of the "industry standard" claims.** Taken from web search results this session, which are **secondary sources** (blog posts, an issue thread, a Go package's docs, third-party guides, and GitHub's own docs seen as a search snippet), not read from the primary specs (OWASP's cheat sheets, Stripe's and GitHub's engineering posts, Google's Play Developer API pages). Where a figure below is only from memory it says so. The choices are conventional and low-risk, but check the primary source before quoting any of them outside this repo.

- **❓34-1 ✅ Token storage and format.** **Store only a plain SHA-256 digest of a 256-bit random secret; show the secret once; prefix it.**
  - *Generate:* `"zpa_" + SecureRandom.urlsafe_base64(32)` (32 random bytes = 256 bits; `zpa_` = "Zealot per-app", so a leaked one is recognisable in a scan and can be registered with a secret scanner later). Never a UUID, never `MD5`, never `rand`.
  - *Store:* `Digest::SHA256.hexdigest(full_secret)` in a **unique-indexed** column, plus `last_four` for the list screen. **No bcrypt/Argon2** (they exist to slow guessing of low-entropy human passwords; a 256-bit random secret cannot be guessed, and a slow hash would only add CPU to every CI call). **No salt and no server-side pepper**: the digest is the lookup key, so it must be deterministic, and a pepper would make rotating it invalidate every token. Sources this session: an issue thread and a developer post describe SHA-256 for high-entropy tokens as common practice (naming Stripe and GitHub), and a Go package documents the same reasoning; the secondary sources disagree only on salting, and the un-salted lookup is the simpler of the two at 256 bits.
  - *Send:* header `Authorization: Bearer <secret>` **only**. The existing `?token=` (the user token) is a known weakness (query strings reach logs and browser history); the new path must not accept it.
  - *Lifetime:* optional `expires_at`; the token screen (34a-7) offers 30 / 90 (default) / 365 days or no expiry (a CI secret that silently expires is a common outage, so "none" stays possible but is labelled). GitHub's fine-grained tokens expire by default (a search result says a 366-day maximum and a 30-day default; from a third-party page, not GitHub's own docs, so unconfirmed). Expiry warnings by email are **not** in this cut (a later slice on the Task 12 mail pipeline).
  - *Limits:* at most **10 live (not revoked, not expired) tokens per app**, so a rotation can overlap (issue the new one, switch CI, revoke the old) and a runaway script cannot mint thousands. The number 10 is this session's choice, not a standard (GitHub's own cap is 50 fine-grained tokens per user, from GitHub's docs snippet).
  - *Revoke:* soft (`revoked_at`), never delete the row, so the future audit log (34c) can still name the token that did something.
- **❓34-2 ✅ Who does a token act as?** **The user who created it, with the token narrowing what that user may do, re-checked on every request.** This is the GitHub fine-grained-token model (a token belongs to a user and can be limited to chosen repositories). A token therefore never has *more* power than its creator has now, and never more than its own app and scope.
  - *Per request:* creator exists, is not `access_locked?`, still passes `manage?(app: token.app)`, and the app is in the request's tenant (`TenantScoped` / `Current.tenant`, 37b-iii-s7c-5). **Fail closed:** any failure is a 401 with one generic message.
  - *Consequence, accepted on purpose:* if the creator is removed from the app, locked or deleted, their CI tokens stop working and the owner issues new ones under someone who still has access. This is the point of a live re-check, not a defect.
  - *Rejected:* a service identity with no user (the model Play's service accounts and GitHub Apps use). It is the better long-term shape for many-app automation but every policy in this app reads `current_user`, so it needs new policy plumbing; revisit if owners ask for tokens that survive staff changes.
  - **Found, not fixed (existing code, outside this task):** `Api::BaseController#validate_user_token` looks a user up by `token` and **does not check `access_locked?`**, so a locked user's user token may still work on `/api` (read from the file, not run). Task 34's new path must check it; whether to close the old one is the operator's call.
- **❓34-3 ✅ Does an "edit" span releases?** **No. Draft-then-publish, one step per call, like GitHub's draft releases**: CI uploads a release as **held** (34a-5), optionally stages and commits a listing draft (34a-3), then explicitly **releases** it (34a-6). Play's atomic multi-part edit is the heavier model; here the held state already gives the same safety, because nothing reaches the signed index until the release call. A CI run that dies between upload and release leaves a visible held release (the release page already has the button), never a half-public one. A "release" step that fails can simply be run again. Revisit only if owners need listing text and a build to go live *together* atomically (that needs a table linking releases to an edit).
  - *To check in 34a-5 before writing code:* what `POST /api/apps/upload` does when the same build is uploaded twice (CI retries). Read `Release.upload_file` and the Task 23 versionCode rules first; if a retry creates a second release, say so in the docs rather than adding idempotency in this slice.
- **❓34-4 ✅ Which token scopes?** **One scope, `publish` (for this one app), stored in a `scopes` column from day one.** Least privilege is the standard (GitHub's docs recommend narrowly scoped tokens); the column costs nothing now and means splitting `publish` into read / upload / release later is a code change, not a migration. Enforcement is by **opt-in allowlist**: a route accepts an app token only if its controller says so and checks the scope, so a new endpoint is closed to tokens by default.
  - *In scope for `publish`:* read the app's own versions (the 34a-2 proof), stage/commit/discard listing text (34a-3), set a channel's track (34a-4), upload a release, optionally held (34a-5), release a held release (34a-6).
  - *Never available to an app token, in any slice:* creating, listing or revoking tokens; collaborators and ownership transfer; archiving or deleting the app; Play credentials and the Play publish/approval flow; store-listing payment and `go_live!`; admin and editorial endpoints; user, device and tenant endpoints. Pulling or halting a release is also **not** in scope (a compromised CI secret should not be able to take an app down); a person does that in the console.

**Not decided here, not needed yet:** rate limits and the audit log are Task 34c; the GitHub Actions example is 34b; both wait on 34a-2.

**34a-1 + 34a-2 result (Storeapp leaf `f.xiv`; built this session on `develop` @ `652bd961`; ruby -c clean, specs written and NOT run).**

- **34a-1:** `app_api_tokens` (migration `20261001100000`), `AppApiToken` (`.issue!`, `.authenticate`, `#revoke!`, `#record_use!`, the `live` scope), `App has_many :api_tokens, dependent: :destroy`. Exactly as carded: `zpa_` + 43 url-safe base64 characters, only the hex SHA-256 stored (unique index), `last_four`, a `scopes` text array defaulting to `{publish}`, soft revoke, at most 10 live tokens per app. No route and no caller of its own.
- **34a-2:** `Api::AppTokenAuth` (included once in `Api::BaseController`, a concern with no `before_action` of its own) and one opt-in, `Api::Apps::VersionsController#index`. `Authorization: Bearer zpa_...` only; `?token=` is never read. On every request: live token with the `publish` scope, creator exists and is not `access_locked?`, and the creator still passes `AppPolicy#update?` for the token's app (that is `manage?(app:)` plus the tenant rule, reused rather than rewritten). Any failure is the same 401 (`api.unauthorized_app_token`, plus `WWW-Authenticate: Bearer`); a valid token on another app's channel is 403. On success `@current_user` is the creator and `last_used_at` is stamped at most once a minute.
- **Choices made, each overrulable:**
  1. **`created_by_id` is nullable, `ON DELETE SET NULL`** (the card said a plain FK). A plain FK would make deleting a user fail while they own a token, and a cascade would erase the row the audit log (34c) wants. A live token with no creator authenticates as nobody (401).
  2. **The check is one SELECT, the stamp is a second, conditional UPDATE.** Liveness (not revoked, not expired) is part of the lookup query, never read and compared afterwards. The stamp is separate because the throttle exists to avoid a write on every call; it also requires the token to still be live, so a just-revoked token is not stamped.
  3. **Only `Bearer zpa_...` counts as an app token.** Any other `Authorization` value (Basic, a bearer with another prefix) is ignored by the opted-in endpoint, so a client that already sends one keeps getting today's answer. A `zpa_` value that fails is a 401 and **never falls back** to the channel key.
  4. **The cap is counted under a row lock on the app** (`App.lock.find` in the issuing transaction), so two simultaneous issues cannot both pass. The refusal is a `RecordInvalid` whose message is English only; 34a-7 must localize it.
  5. **`issue!` returns `AppApiToken::Issued` (`token`, `secret`)**, the secret exists nowhere else.
  6. **No CHECK constraints** (scopes non-empty, digest length) in the migration, on purpose: `db/schema.rb` is hand-edited here and a check on a `varchar` column dumps in a form I cannot confirm without Postgres. The model validates both.
  7. **What the proof endpoint proves:** the versions endpoint still needs `channel_key`, so a token adds nothing a channel key did not already give there. It proves the auth path, the 401s and the 403, not a privilege.
- **Departs from Storeapp's own text for `f.xiv`, recorded so nobody is surprised:** that text sketches a dedicated `POST /api/v1/publish`. This board's decisions (34-1 to 34-4) picked per-app tokens on the existing `/api` behind an opt-in allowlist, and that is what was built. The two doors still share no code: the token path is a bearer header, the console path is a session cookie, and a token cannot open any session page.
- **Verified how:** `ruby -c` on all nine Ruby files touched or added; both locale files load as YAML and carry the two new keys; a stdlib-only script confirmed that 20,000 generated secrets all match `SECRET_FORMAT` (47 characters), the bearer-header parser accepts `Bearer zpa_...` in any case and ignores Basic, a non-`zpa_` bearer, nil and a short or wrong-prefix secret, and the digest is 64 hex characters. **Not verified:** the migration, `db/schema.rb` (hand-edited: the array default dumping as `default: ["publish"], null: false, array: true`, and the column and index order, are from knowledge of Rails' dumper, so the `db/schema.rb matches migrations` job is the check), the model and request specs (`spec/models/app_api_token_spec.rb`, `spec/requests/api_app_token_spec.rb`, 17 examples each, never run), and anything under Rails or Postgres.
- **Flagged forward:**
  1. **No endpoint can publish with a token yet.** `POST /api/apps/upload` still takes only the user token, and no slice card says it opts in; **34a-5 must say so and do it.** When it does, `spec/requests/manual_upload_only_spec.rb`'s `upload_doors` line for the upload controller (`before_action :validate_user_token`) is a deliberate edit, not a side effect.
  2. **Until 34a-7 the only way to create a token is a Rails console call to `AppApiToken.issue!`.** Nothing in the app can show, list or revoke one.
  3. **The old user-token path is unchanged:** it still reaches every app that user can write to and still does not check `access_locked?` (decision 34-2's found-not-fixed item; the operator's call).
  4. **No rate limit and no audit log** (34c), so a leaked token is only stopped by revoking it.
  5. **Expiry is checked, but nothing warns before it** (not in this cut, by decision 34-1).

**Choices made, each overrulable.**
1. **New door, header only.** `Api::UserTokenHeaderAuth` reads `Authorization: Bearer <user token>`, refuses a `zpa_` value and an `access_locked?` user, one generic 401. `?token=` is not read on these two endpoints (decision 34-1's weakness). The old `validate_user_token` is untouched (operator's call, decision 34-2).
2. **`platform_admin?` not `admin?`.** `AndroidSigningKeyPolicy` now allows only an admin on the default host (4b-b). The policy is asked on the class before the key is looked up, so a non-admin cannot learn whether a key exists. The admin console behaves the same on the default host.
3. **DELETE needs `checksum`** equal to the current key's. 1 MB keystore cap (a choice). Keytool missing is 503, a keystore keytool rejects is 422.
4. **`filter_parameters` gains `keystore` and `service_account_json`.** Found: the Play credential API posts the service-account JSON as a body string, which no filter matched, so it could reach the log. One-word fix.
5. **The expiry choices are read from `Apps::ApiTokensController`**, one definition. Token create, revoke and the signing key change each write one log line (who, which, never a secret) until 34c's audit log exists.
6. **The script's two GET lookups** (`/api/apps`) still send the user token in the query string, because the old endpoint reads nothing else. Every other call and every secret avoids argv and URLs.

**Not done, flagged.** No rate limit (34c). Two simultaneous signing-key creates could both pass `only_one_record` (no unique index; same as `PlayCredential`). Whether `keytool` is in the Render image is unchecked. **Not verified:** everything. Nothing was run, not even `ruby -c` or `bash -n`; the three new specs and the script have never executed. Only the two locale files were loaded as YAML.

**Debug run (2026-10-03, operator-directed, no task; first run of `bin/bootstrap-publishing`, a `--dry-run` in Termux).** Bash stopped with "line 349: unexpected EOF while looking for matching" a single quote, before any call to Zealot, so nothing was read or changed. Cause, read from the file and not run: the log line after a token is stored had an apostrophe inside a double-quoted alternate expansion (`${GITHUB_REPO:+ as $GITHUB_REPO's secret ...}`); bash 5 takes it as an opening single quote and reads to the end of the file. Every other apostrophe in the script is inside plain double quotes, a comment or the quoted `EOF` heredoc, which are safe. **Fix:** that line now builds a `where` string from plain assignments; same output, slightly different wording. **Still not run, no `bash -n`:** a second syntax or runtime error would only show on the next run.

**34d-4 (D-Store leaf 38, `7.a.xii.zo`; 2026-10-03, operator-directed, written, NOT run).** Why it reads a web page: there is no password-to-token API, so the script makes the two page loads a browser makes (`GET /users/sign_in`, `POST /users/sign_in`, `GET /users/edit`) with a throwaway cookie jar and takes the 32-hex value of the "API Token" input. **Facts read from the code, not run:** (1) the login form registers an email it does not know (a typo makes a stray account), as a developer, if `Setting.registrations_enabled`; (2) **no new sign-up can be the admin**: only `User.admin_signup_email` (env `ZEALOT_ADMIN_SIGNUP_EMAIL`, default in the source `bossblingzs@gmail.com`) can be created as admin, and only through the admin entry (`admin_entry=1`), so the signing key step needs that account; I did not work around this; (3) `config.maximum_attempts = 5`, so the script makes one attempt and never retries; (4) `ApplicationController` calls `skip_before_action :verify_authenticity_token` right after `protect_from_forgery`, so the login form is not CSRF-checked today; the script still sends the page's CSRF token when there is one, so it keeps working if that is switched back on. **Choices, each overrulable:** the generated password is 36 random bytes from `openssl rand` (else `/dev/urandom`), base64, 48 characters, saved only to a new 0600 file the operator names; a login that fails removes that file again; `--dry-run` refuses `--new-password-file` because the login would create the account; the user token is never saved (it is read again each run). **Not done:** a dedicated non-admin account that owns Storeapp and the CI token (least privilege): today the admin makes the per-app token, which then acts as that admin account (decision 34-2). **Not verified:** the HTML patterns (`<input … clipboard-center-target="source" … value="…">`, `<meta name="csrf-token">`) were read from the Slim views, not from a rendered page.

**34d-5 (D-Store leaf 39, `7.a.xiii.zi`; 2026-10-03, operator-directed, written, NOT run).** The operator's architecture: the admin (`ZEALOT_ADMIN_SIGNUP_EMAIL`, default `bossblingzs@gmail.com`) is the organisation and holds the signing key; it does not publish. A separate developer account owns Storeapp and publishes it; the organisation signs automatically. **Read from the code, not run:** (1) signing happens in Zealot when it processes an uploaded `.aab` (`AnthropicAssetDeliveryJob` -> `AssetPackService` -> `BundletoolService`, key `AndroidSigningKey.current`, the same key for every app), and Storeapp's `release-aab.yml` builds the bundle unsigned, so the developer's token never touches the key; (2) the developer account is made by the login form when `Setting.registrations_enabled` is true (default from `ZEALOT_REGISTER_ENABLED`, `true`), as role `developer`; the admin email can never be made that way; (3) `AppPolicy#create?` is `manage?`, true for any developer, `App#create_owner` makes the creator the app's owner, and `AppApiToken` acts as its creator (decision 34-2); (4) the admin keeps authority over every app through its role, so no collaborator row for the admin was added. **Change:** `--only signing-key|app` is required. The signing key run (admin) takes `--sign-in <admin email> --admin-entry` or a token and the keystore options, and refuses `--app-name`, `--bundle-id`, `--github-repo`, `--secret-out` and `--rotate`. The app run (developer) does steps 4a to 4c and refuses `--admin-entry` and every keystore option. The old single run is gone, because it would have made the admin the owner. **Needs the operator:** a developer email they can receive mail at; registrations enabled on the server (else the admin must create the account); the keystore file. **Not verified:** nothing was run, not even `bash -n`; the apostrophe-in-`${VAR:+...}` pattern that broke the first run was grepped for and is absent. **Found, not fixed:** if the signing key is missing or `bundletool` is absent, the job logs and skips, and the release is saved with `signed: false`, so a missing key shows up only on the release page.

**34d-6 (D-Store leaf 40, `7.a.xiii.zo`; 2026-10-03, found on the operator's first `--only app` run, written, NOT run).** The run with `--sign-in claudeone7492@gmail.com --new-password-file` answered 422 and the script blamed the email or the password length, which was a guess: the generated password is 48 characters. Read from the code: `ApplicationController` has `protect_from_forgery with: :exception` and `ExceptionHandler` maps `InvalidAuthenticityToken` to 422, while `Users::SessionsController#register_unknown_user` renders the login page with status 422 when the new account fails validation. So 422 has two possible causes the script could not tell apart. **Change:** `explain_sign_in_422` reads the answer page and prints either the anti-forgery refusal (no account touched, no lockout count) or the validation phrases (`Email ...`, `Password ...`, `Username ...`); the CSRF token is also read from the form's hidden `authenticity_token` input when the meta tag is missing, with a log line when neither is found. **Not verified:** nothing was run, not even `bash -n`; the apostrophe-in-`${VAR:+...}` pattern was grepped for and is absent. **Still unknown:** which of the two causes it was; the next run's message will say.

**34d-7 (D-Store leaf 41, `7.a.xiii.zu`; 2026-10-03, found on the operator's second `--only app` run, written, NOT run).** The 34d-6 message answered "the page gave no reason that could be read". **Read from the live server (the login page only, a plain GET):** registrations are open (the page shows the `new_here` hint, in Chinese: the server's default locale is `zh-CN`, `DEFAULT_LOCALE` is unset), so a closed sign-up is not the cause. **Read from the code:** `config/initializers/devise.rb` sets `responder.error_status = :unprocessable_entity`, so a FAILED sign-in (wrong password for an account that already exists) also answers 422 with the login page and a flash message; the script's comment that a wrong password is a redirect was wrong, and its English phrase matching could not read a Chinese flash. **Change:** `explain_sign_in_422` prints the page `<title>` and the flash text (`data-controller="notification"`) as the page shows them. **Not verified:** nothing was run, not even `bash -n`. **Still unknown:** whether the email already has an account or the new account failed validation; the next run prints the page's own message.

**34d-8 (debug run, no D-Store leaf; 2026-10-03, found from the Render request log of the operator's third `--only app` run, written, NOT run).** The third run printed "the anti-forgery (CSRF) token was refused before any account was touched". **The request log says otherwise** (`render-signin.log`, 10:09 UTC, deploy `83b618e`): `GET /users/sign_in` 200; `POST /users/sign_in` `Users::SessionsController#create` with `status=0` (a Warden throw, not a response), then `POST /users/sign_in` `#new` 200 (Devise's failure app re-rendering the login page, which the client sees as 422). A refused CSRF token raises before `create` runs, so the token was accepted. **Cause of the wrong message, read from the code:** `explain_sign_in_422` tested the whole page for the word `authenticity`, and the login form always carries a hidden `authenticity_token` input, so every failed sign-in matched. **Second finding:** `register_unknown_user` registers an unknown email and then lets Devise sign it in, so the same POST can leave an account behind; the script deleted the generated password file after every failed run, so an account may now exist with a password nobody has. **Change:** the CSRF branch tests only the page's title and flash text for `verify CSRF` or `InvalidAuthenticityToken`; the generated password file is kept once the POST has been sent (`SIGN_IN_POSTED`), with a line saying to use `--password-file` next. **Not verified:** nothing was run, not even `bash -n`. **Still unknown, and the next run prints it:** why Devise refused the login. Candidates read from the code, none seen: the account exists with another password (earlier runs, password files deleted); the account is locked (`:lockable`, five wrong passwords, `unlock_in` one hour); sign-ups closed for this email. **Account state is unknown:** `claudeone7492@gmail.com` may or may not exist.

**34d-9 (debug run, no D-Store leaf; 2026-10-03, operator-directed, written, NOT run; `bash -n` was run on the script, syntax only, exit 0).** The operator asked for the admin (whose password the operator knows) to fix the possibly stray developer account instead of making the login form overwrite passwords. **The login form stays as it is on purpose:** it is public, and letting it replace an existing account's password would let anyone take over any account by knowing its email (the controller's own comment says an existing email is never touched). **Read from the code, so no server change was needed:** `Api::UsersController` (admin only through `UserPolicy`) has `GET /api/users/search?email=`, `PUT /api/users/:id` (permits `password`) and `DELETE /api/users/:id/unlock`; it reads the user token as a `token` field, like `/api/apps`. **Change:** `--only developer --sign-in <admin email> --password-file F --developer-email E --developer-password-file NEWFILE`: searches for E; none found means nothing is done and the message says to register it with `--only app --new-password-file`; found means a random 48-character password is made, saved in the new file (mode 0600), set with the PUT (the file is removed again if Zealot refuses it), and the account is unlocked. **Choices, each overrulable:** it resets the password rather than deleting and re-creating the account (same result for the sign-in, and nothing owned by the account is lost; deleting is `DELETE /api/users/:id` or the admin Users screen); it never creates an account (a mistyped email would register a stray one) and refuses `--new-password-file` for that reason; `UserSerializer` returns no role, so it cannot refuse an admin account, it only refuses the email it signed in with; the new password is never in argv. **Not verified:** nothing was run against a server; the three routes were read, not called; whether the admin account exists and its password is the operator's word. **Production users** are not affected: they use forgot-password (`:recoverable`); whether Zealot can send that mail was not checked.

#### 🟡 Task 36b — register every signed app with Google, for every tenant (discovery done; 36b-1 to 36b-7 BUILT, written, NOT run; 36b-8 and 36b-9 parked; **registration is OFF until `ADC_AUTO_REGISTER=true`**)

**Operator direction (this session, in the operator's words condensed):** the apps are never published to Google Play or the Apple App Store, only to the organisation's own store and appstore. The Play credentials were already supplied. Every app deployed through Zealot, **for every tenant and white-label operator, is to be signed automatically with the organisation's key and its package name registered automatically under the organisation's verified Google developer account.** "Check the API for the credentials so all apps are signed and registered automatically."

**Read first: `docs/android_developer_console_api.md`.** It holds the full method table, messages, enumerations, the registration flow, the operator's credential setup and what was and was not proved. This section is the plan; that file is the evidence.

**What the discovery established (each item is tagged in the doc):**
1. **The Play service account cannot be used.** The Android Developer Console API takes OAuth 2.0 only; service accounts, Workload Identity Federation and API keys are refused. The credential needed is an OAuth client plus a refresh token granted by the account that owns the developer account.
2. **That credential now exists.** The operator made a Desktop OAuth client, enabled the API in the Cloud project and granted a refresh token with the right scope. It is in the operator's Termux environment and in Render on `zealot-web` as `CLIENT_ID`, `CLIENT_SECRET`, `ADC_REFRESH_TOKEN`. **Live calls proved:** token refresh works, the developer account (`EDGES ENTERPRISE LTD`) is `VERIFIED`, and the package list can be read (one package, `com.antropic`, `REGISTERED`).
3. **Google's definition was read** (it needs an API key, `ADC_API_KEY`, kept in Termux only). Every method, message and enumeration is in the doc. **No write call has ever been made.**
4. **Signing already does not depend on the tenant.** `AndroidSigningKey` is one org-wide row used by `AnthropicAssetDeliveryJob` for every `.aab`, whoever the tenant is. `TenantSigningKey` is limited by a database constraint to the purpose `catalog_index`, so tenant keys sign the index, never an APK. **No tenant-specific signing code is needed.**
5. **Two gaps in "everything is signed".** (a) Only `.aab` uploads are signed by Zealot; a directly uploaded `.apk` keeps its uploader's signature. (b) `signed` and `signing_key_checksum` on `releases` say which key signed; registration must only claim the org key for a release where `signing_key_checksum` equals the current key's checksum.
6. **Registering is tenant-blind on purpose, which is an identity decision, not a code detail.** The verified developer on record will be the organisation for every tenant's package names. See ❓36-1.
7. **Google's enforcement reading in Task 27h may be out of date.** See the first section of the doc. It changes urgency, not the plan.

**❓ Decisions. The operator told the implementing session to answer every question "with industry standards approaches". The answers below are therefore the session's, applied in the code, and the operator may overrule any of them (each is a small, local change).**

| ❓ | Question | Answer (industry practice; built as written) | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|---|
| 36-1 | The organisation becomes Google's registered owner of **every tenant's** package names. Is that acceptable to the tenants (contracts, a tenant leaving later)? | **Build as directed** (the operator asked for exactly this). Keep one row per package (36b-3) with the app and tenant it came from, so a later transfer (Google has a `PENDING_TRANSFER` state) can be done per package. | **This reverses the stated scope in `AndroidSigningKey`'s header comment ("not a re-signing service for third-party apps") and the Task 5 decision text.** One shared key also means one compromise affects every tenant; that trade-off was accepted for Task 5 and is repeated here. A tenant that leaves cannot take its signing identity with it. |
| 36-2 | A package name Google already knows (`SELECT_KEY_FROM_LIST`) needs proof of key ownership and possibly a justification. What should Zealot do? | **Register new package names only. For a known one, record `needs_review` with Google's answer and stop.** Never auto-justify, never auto-prove (36b-8 and 36b-9 are separate, later, operator-triggered). | Re-signing an app that users already have installed with the org key would break their updates. A wrong claim on someone else's package name is a policy problem. |
| 36-3 | When does automatic registration run? | **Only when `ADC_AUTO_REGISTER=true` in the environment. Absent or anything else = off.** Also `ADC_DRY_RUN=true` logs the request it would send and sends nothing. | The first deploy of the code must change nothing; the first real write is the operator's choice. |
| 36-4 | Which releases trigger it? | **A release that Zealot signed with the current org key** (`signed` and `signing_key_checksum == AndroidSigningKey.current.checksum`), after `AnthropicAssetDeliveryJob` records it. Best effort, never blocks an upload, same posture as that job. | Avoids claiming the org key for an `.apk` signed by someone else. |
| 36-5 | Which field is the package name? | **`app.play_package_name.presence || release.bundle_id`**; the session reads both columns in the code and on a few rows before relying on either. | Not checked this session. |
| 36-6 | More than one developer account on the OAuth identity, or none verified? | **Act only if exactly one account is returned and it is `VERIFIED`; otherwise log and do nothing.** The account id is read at run time, never stored in code. | Prevents registering under a wrong account. |
| 36-7 | Registering is done by a background job outside tenant scoping. | **The job reads `App` unscoped. Tenant scopes and policy scopes are for what a person may see, not for this job.** Viewing the result in the console stays tenant-scoped (36b-7). | A tenant-scoped read would silently skip every tenant's apps. |

**Order the operator should follow (each step is reversible except the last):**
1. Apply the patch and push. It redeploys Zealot, so do it when no bundle is compiling. **Migrate** (the new table). Nothing else changes: `ADC_AUTO_REGISTER` is unset, so nothing is registered.
2. From a Rails console on the service (Render shell), run `bin/rails google_adc:inventory`. It only reads. Send the output. It also answers, for the first time, whether `keys.list` returns the 403 other developers reported.
3. Run `ADC_DRY_RUN=true bin/rails "google_adc:register[PACKAGE]"` for ONE package name you own. It reads, prints what it would send and saves nothing.
4. Run it again without `ADC_DRY_RUN` for the same package. This is the first write to Google. If Google answers 400, the log line `[GoogleAdc] 400 for POST ...` carries the full body: send it.
5. Only after steps 2 to 4 behave: set `ADC_AUTO_REGISTER=true` on `zealot-web`. Every newly signed release then enqueues a registration.

**Order and why.** 36b-1 and 36b-2 first, because they prove the unknowns with **reads** before any slice writes. Until a real `keys.list` and `getRegistrationPolicy` have been seen, 36b-5 is a guess. 36b-3 and 36b-4 are independent of each other and of 36b-2. Nothing here depends on Task 37/38 code, and nothing needs `apps.tenant_id` to be set.

**What deploying this patch does to production:** one new empty table and a badge that appears only once a registration row exists. `ADC_AUTO_REGISTER` is unset, so no release enqueues anything. No existing behaviour changes.

**Not verified (still true after the build):** any write call; `keys.list` and `getRegistrationPolicy` (never called); the Status API with a good key; what `registeredAppStore` means; whether the consent screen is in "Testing" (refresh tokens would then expire after 7 days); the SHA-256 fingerprint of the org key (an earlier session reported it, this one did not recompute it); who owns `com.antropic` and which key it uses; which of `apps.play_package_name` and `releases.bundle_id` holds the real package name; that Google's rollout reaches installs from Zealot's store. No Rails, database or spec was run. 36b-1 to 36b-7 are written code that nothing has executed.

**Needs the operator:**
1. Apply the patch and follow the five steps under "Order the operator should follow". Overrule ❓36-1 or ❓36-2 if the answers above are wrong for your contracts.
2. Put `ADC_API_KEY` into Render on `zealot-web` **only if** 36b-2 should call the Status API (it is in Termux today). Setting a Render variable redeploys the service, so do it between Zealot builds, as with every other Render change.
3. Check the OAuth consent screen's publishing status (Testing or In production) in the Cloud console and set it to In production, so the refresh token does not lapse after 7 days.
4. Delete any leftover API keys in the Cloud console other than the one named `zealot-adc`.
5. Optionally say which tenants and which package names exist today, so 36b-2's first inventory can be read against reality.

**s7 survey result (this session; read from `develop` @ `e0f765e1`, `config/routes.rb` and the controllers named; nothing run).**

*Headline finding: `env['zealot.tenant']` has NO reader anywhere in `app/`.* `config/initializers/tenant_host.rb` sets it, `lib/zealot/tenant_resolver.rb` computes it, and only the catalog-index code (`KeyResolver`, `App.for_tenant`) understands tenants, from an explicit argument, never from the request. So today no request-time read is tenant-scoped, and nothing needs to be to stay correct: `apps.tenant_id` is never set, so every app is in the default catalog. The table is what must change **before anything sets `apps.tenant_id`**.

*Second finding: Zealot serves no public app-listing page.* The public storefront is D-store (Task 26). Every page that lists apps here is the authenticated console (or guest mode, an operator setting). So the leak surface is (a) the console, which is an operator/team tool, not a tenant-facing store, and (b) two unauthenticated spots below. Whether the console itself must be tenant-partitioned (a tenant operator logging in to Zealot and seeing only their apps) is a product question the board has never asked: **new ❓4a**.

| # | Route(s) | Reads | Who can reach it | Tenant-relevant? | Proposed slice |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `GET /` (`home#index`, `landing_stats`) | `App.count`, `Release.count`, added to a fixed baseline | **Anyone, no login** | **Yes, a count leak.** It counts tenants' apps and releases into a public number. No app data, just a total. | **s7a ✅ (built, see "s7a result")**: count `App.for_tenant(nil)` (and releases through it) so a tenant's apps never move the default site's public number. One method, no migration. |
| 2 | `GET /api/apps/latest`, `versions`, `version_exist`, `POST upload` (`validate_channel_key`) | The channel found by `Channel.find_by(key:)` | Holder of a channel key | **No.** Scoped by an unguessable per-channel key, not by host. A key for tenant A's channel can only read tenant A's app. | none. Note only: keep it host-independent. |
| 3 | `GET /:channel`, `/:channel/:id`, `/:channel/versions`, `release_types`, `branches`, `/download/releases/:id` | `Channel.friendly.find(slug)` then its releases | Anyone who knows the slug, unless a password is set; guest mode opens more | **Partly.** Reachable by slug on any host.
